title: Confiscation orders: not part of the sentence, but may affect it
statement: The Confiscation Act 1997 is the primary mechanism (other legislation may also require confiscation). A confiscation order is not part of the sentence but imposed in addition; forfeiture can mitigate where it puts the offender in a worse position than before the offending (punitive and deterrent) — but see anc.confiscation.effect_on_sentence: orders disgorging profits are not considered, and the automatic forfeiture of a serious drug offender’s property must not be taken into account. Applications are best heard with or close to sentence. On appeal, confiscation orders are treated as part of the sentence.

refs.q: A confiscation order is not part of a sentence. It is imposed in addition to the sentence.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation

refs.q: Forfeiture – whether by order or automatically under the Confiscation Act or via the operation of another piece of legislation – can be a mitigating factor where it places an offender in a worse position than before the offending and so is punitive and deterrent.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation

refs.q: Because a confiscation order may affect the exercise of the sentencing discretion, it is best if an application seeking one is heard contemporaneously with or as close as possible to passing sentence.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation

refs.q: On appeal, confiscation orders are treated as if they were part of the sentence.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation

refs.q: The Confiscation Act 1997 (Vic) (‘Confiscation Act’) is the primary mechanism for confiscating the proceeds and instruments of crime in Victoria, although there is other legislation that may also require a court to make a confiscation order.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation

refs.q: A confiscation order may take a variety of forms.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation

refs.q: This chapter is included in this manual only because there are difficult questions about the interaction of confiscation legislation with the sentencing principles and purposes.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation

refs.q: To the extent separation is possible, this chapter is restricted to issues relevant to a sentencing court and to confiscation orders that may be imposed at the time of sentencing.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation

title: Forfeiture orders and pecuniary penalty orders
statement: On conviction of a Schedule 1 offence (including a Schedule 2 offence) the court may, on application, order forfeiture of “tainted property” (specifying interests) or defer sentencing until the application is determined; property may be restrained around the time of charge. On application it may make a pecuniary penalty order equal to the benefits derived (reducible by restitution or compensation paid), and may defer sentence until that is determined. The Manual identifies Schedule 1/2 offences only for drug and property offences (28.7, 27.5.1: guide.drugs.statutory_schemes, guide.property.statutory_schemes); for other offences, (app policy) membership (and whether an application has been or will be made) must come from the user.

refs.q: Firstly, if an offender is convicted of a Schedule 1 offence (which includes a Schedule 2 offence) a court may, on application, make a forfeiture order for ‘tainted property’ or it may defer sentencing until after determining the forfeiture application.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation > 17.1 – Statutory regime > 17.1.1 – Available orders

refs.q: Secondly, a court may, on application, make a pecuniary penalty order (‘PPO’) requiring the offender to pay the State a penalty equal to the value of any ‘benefits’ they derived from committing the offence. The court has the discretion to reduce this by any amount paid as restitution or compensation, and may also defer sentencing until after determination of the pecuniary penalty application.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation > 17.1 – Statutory regime > 17.1.1 – Available orders

refs.q: The order must specify the interests in the property to which it applies.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation > 17.1 – Statutory regime > 17.1.1 – Available orders

refs.q: A court may also restrain ‘tainted property’ at or closely before the time of charge. This prevents the accused from disposing of tainted property in anticipation of being convicted of the relevant offending.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation > 17.1 – Statutory regime > 17.1.1 – Available orders

refs.q: At the time of sentencing for a Victorian offence, a court has two primary options.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation > 17.1 – Statutory regime > 17.1.1 – Available orders

refs.q: A forfeiture order directs that the ‘tainted property’, or any part of it specified by the court, be forfeited to the Minister.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation > 17.1 – Statutory regime > 17.1.1 – Available orders

title: Automatic forfeiture (Schedule 2 offences; serious drug offenders)
statement: On conviction of a Schedule 2 offence where a restraining order was made and no exclusion order has been made, the property is automatically forfeited 60 days after the restraining order or conviction, whichever is later. Almost all property of declared serious drug offenders is automatically forfeited.

refs.q: If a person is convicted of a Schedule 2 offence under the Confiscation Act and an order was previously made restraining disposition of the property, and no exclusion order has been made, then the property is automatically forfeited to the Minister 60 days after the restraining order is made or the offender is convicted, whichever is later. The statutory scheme also provides for the automatic forfeiture of almost all property of offenders declared to be ‘serious drug offenders’ under the Sentencing Act 1991 (Vic) (‘the Act’).
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation > 17.1 – Statutory regime > 17.1.2 – Automatic forfeiture

title: “Tainted property” and “benefits”
statement: Tainted property: property used or intended to be used in or in connection with the offence, or derived or realised from it or from the offence. “Used” has its ordinary meaning, and property is “used” only when it, or some feature of it, is turned towards bringing about the offender’s purpose; “in connection with” widens it; connection is a matter of degree and fact (no substantial connection needed); the nature and significance of use bear on the discretion; merely doing an act in or on property is normally insufficient; passive use makes connection less likely. Benefits (for PPOs) include money received (regardless of expenses), property derived, services or advantages, increases in property value, profits from depictions of the offence, and anything else the court considers appropriate.

refs.q: • used or intended to be used in or in connection with the offence; • derived or realised directly or indirectly from such property; or • derived or realised directly or indirectly from the commission of the offence.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation > 17.1 – Statutory regime > 17.1.3 – ‘Tainted property’

refs.q: In considering if property is tainted, the Court of Appeal has made the following observations about the statutory definition: • The term ‘used’ should be given its ordinary meaning – that is, employed or made use of for a particular purpose or end. • The definition is wide and inclusion of ‘in connection with’ extends the definition of tainted property to beyond that used in committing the offence. • Whether there is a connection between use of the property and commission of the crime is a question of degree and fact. There does not need to be a substantial connection, nor does it need to be shown the offence could only have been committed with the property. • The nature, extent, and significance of the use of the property in connection with the commission of the crime are relevant to the court in determining whether to exercise its discretion to order its forfeiture.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation > 17.1 – Statutory regime > 17.1.3 – ‘Tainted property’

refs.q: The question of whether the property was ‘used’ will often be decisive, but the mere fact that an act was done in or on particular property is normally not sufficient to bring it within the definition of ‘tainted property’.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation > 17.1 – Statutory regime > 17.1.3 – ‘Tainted property’

refs.q: The more passive the property’s use, the less likely it is the relevant connection will be found.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation > 17.1 – Statutory regime > 17.1.3 – ‘Tainted property’

refs.q: any money received as a result of the commission of the offence, regardless of any expenditures incurred;
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation > 17.1 – Statutory regime > 17.1.4 – ‘Benefits’

refs.q: any other thing the court considers appropriate.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation > 17.1 – Statutory regime > 17.1.4 – ‘Benefits’

refs.q: The definition of ‘tainted property’ includes property: • used or intended to be used in or in connection with the offence; • derived or realised directly or indirectly from such property; or • derived or realised directly or indirectly from the commission of the offence.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation > 17.1 – Statutory regime > 17.1.3 – ‘Tainted property’

refs.q: It is only when the property or some feature of it is turned towards bringing about the offender’s purpose that it can be said to have been ‘used’.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation > 17.1 – Statutory regime > 17.1.3 – ‘Tainted property’

refs.q: For the purpose of determining the quantum of a PPO, the ‘benefits’ of offending include: • any money received as a result of the commission of the offence, regardless of any expenditures incurred; • any property derived or realised, directly or indirectly, by the offender or another at the offender’s request or direction, as the result of the offence; • any benefit, service, or financial advantage provided for the offender or another person, at the request or direction of the offender, as the result of the commission of the offence; • any increase in the total value of property in which the offender has an interest immediately before the commission of the offence and ending after the commission of the offence that was due to the commission of the offence; • any profits derived by the offender, or by another person on behalf of the offender or at the offender’s request or direction, from a depiction of the offence in an entertainment medium; • any other thing the court considers appropriate.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation > 17.1 – Statutory regime > 17.1.4 – ‘Benefits’

title: Magistrates’ and Children’s Court limits on confiscation
statement: The Magistrates’ and Children’s Courts may not make forfeiture orders over real property, or orders whose value exceeds the Magistrates’ Court civil jurisdictional limit (unless personal injury damages are claimed); the Supreme or County Court may then make the order.

refs.q: The Magistrates’ and Children’s Courts have limited jurisdiction to make confiscation orders. Relevant to sentencing, they may not: • make a forfeiture order in respect of real property; • in relation to the conviction of an offender for a particular offence, make a forfeiture order in respect of property, or a PPO, whose value exceeds the jurisdictional limit of the Magistrates’ Court in civil proceedings, unless personal injury damages are claimed.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation > 17.1 – Statutory regime > 17.1.5 – Jurisdiction

refs.q: In these circumstances, the Supreme Court or County Court may make the necessary order.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation > 17.1 – Statutory regime > 17.1.5 – Jurisdiction

title: Considerations for forfeiture of tainted property
statement: Considerations include use of the property; hardship to anyone; others’ claims; value; nature and gravity of offending; involvement and history; other property confiscated; the penalty; the offender’s interest; drug value or crop size; acquisition with drug proceeds; utility to the offender; involvement in the offence; deterrence; and effect on rehabilitation. The discretion is broad.

refs.q: • the use that is made, or is ordinarily intended to be made, of the property; • any hardship the order is reasonably likely to cause anyone; • the claim of any person to an interest in the property; • the value of the property; • the nature and gravity of the offending; • the degree of the offender’s involvement and their criminal history; • the value of any other property confiscated; • the penalty imposed; • the nature of the offender’s interest in the property; • the value of any drugs involved or the size of the crop; • whether the property was acquired with proceeds from the sale of drugs; • the utility of the property to the offender; • the extent of the property’s involvement with the commission of the offence; • the deterrent purpose of forfeiture; and • the extent to which retention of the property might bear on the offender’s rehabilitation.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation > 17.1 – Statutory regime > 17.1.6 – Relevant considerations

refs.q: Only some of these factors are legislatively mandated, but the multiplicity of principles to be considered, and their continued viability, indicates that the court’s discretion is broad and multi-faceted when making a confiscation order.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation > 17.1 – Statutory regime > 17.1.6 – Relevant considerations

refs.q: In determining whether to make a forfeiture order for tainted property, a court may consider: • the use that is made, or is ordinarily intended to be made, of the property; • any hardship the order is reasonably likely to cause anyone; • the claim of any person to an interest in the property; • the value of the property; • the nature and gravity of the offending; • the degree of the offender’s involvement and their criminal history; • the value of any other property confiscated; • the penalty imposed; • the nature of the offender’s interest in the property; • the value of any drugs involved or the size of the crop; • whether the property was acquired with proceeds from the sale of drugs; • the utility of the property to the offender; • the extent of the property’s involvement with the commission of the offence; • the deterrent purpose of forfeiture; and • the extent to which retention of the property might bear on the offender’s rehabilitation.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation > 17.1 – Statutory regime > 17.1.6 – Relevant considerations

title: Confiscation and sentence: proportionality, punishment, remorse and cooperation
statement: Proportionality requires due consideration of confiscation, but it is not always mitigating: does it have a disproportionate or deterrent effect? Forfeiture must be proportionate (unacceptable hardship can be critical). Orders disgorging profits are not considered; forfeiture of lawfully acquired property or PPOs exceeding profits may be; automatic forfeiture of a serious drug offender’s property must not be taken into account. Confiscation beyond profits is punishment and failing to consider it may be error; possible future forfeiture is considered with sufficient evidence, the offender bearing the burden on the balance of probabilities (credible material on lawful source; proof of loss beyond profits). A forfeiture order may indicate remorse or cooperation (no deeming); cooperation requires conscious facilitation, not a pragmatic decision.

refs.q: Proportionality requires due consideration of any confiscation order, but it will not always be a mitigating factor. The question is whether confiscation will have a disproportionate (or deterrent) effect on the offender.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation > 17.2 – Interaction with sentencing principles and purposes > 17.2.1 – Proportionality

refs.q: It distinguishes between orders disgorging the profits of crime, which are not to be considered, and orders directing the forfeiture of lawfully acquired property or a PPO relating to benefits that exceed the profits of the offence, which may both be taken into consideration in determining an appropriate sentence. The Act also prohibits a court from taking into account the automatic forfeiture of a serious drug offender’s property.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation > 17.2 – Interaction with sentencing principles and purposes > 17.2.1 – Proportionality

refs.q: If confiscation does more than deprive an offender of the profits of crime, it constitutes punishment and can be considered by the court in determining an appropriate sentence. The failure to do so may constitute error.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation > 17.2 – Interaction with sentencing principles and purposes > 17.2.2 – Punishment

refs.q: However, there must be sufficient evidence for the court to consider the likely effect on the offender, and an offender relying on this point in mitigation has the burden of persuading the court on the balance of probabilities.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation > 17.2 – Interaction with sentencing principles and purposes > 17.2.2 – Punishment

refs.q: An offender must present ‘credible material’ identifying the property’s source, so the court may positively conclude that at least a substantial portion was lawfully acquired.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation > 17.2 – Interaction with sentencing principles and purposes > 17.2.2 – Punishment

refs.q: The Act allows the court to consider a forfeiture order as indicative of remorse or cooperation. However, the weight to be given to it will turn on the facts of the case and the Act is not to be read as creating some kind of deeming provision, such that compliance with any relevant order is evidence of remorse or cooperation.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation > 17.2 – Interaction with sentencing principles and purposes > 17.2.3 – Remorse and cooperation

refs.q: For an offender’s conduct in relation to confiscation proceedings to constitute cooperation, the conduct must be something more than a pragmatic decision and must involve the offender consciously facilitating resolution of the proceedings.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation > 17.2 – Interaction with sentencing principles and purposes > 17.2.3 – Remorse and cooperation

refs.q: The Act limits the manner in which a court may consider confiscation.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation > 17.2 – Interaction with sentencing principles and purposes > 17.2.1 – Proportionality

refs.q: Any forfeiture order must be proportionate to the nature and gravity of the offence and the offender’s circumstances. This can be the critical consideration if ordering forfeiture would cause unacceptable hardship.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation > 17.2 – Interaction with sentencing principles and purposes > 17.2.1 – Proportionality

refs.q: Similarly, if an offender alleges they have lost benefits in excess of profits derived from the crime, they must produce evidence for the court to make a positive determination on the balance of probabilities.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation > 17.2 – Interaction with sentencing principles and purposes > 17.2.2 – Punishment

refs.q: Moreover, if lawfully acquired property is used in the commission of a crime and becomes ‘tainted property’, the punitive element of its forfeiture must be sufficiently identified for the court.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation > 17.2 – Interaction with sentencing principles and purposes > 17.2.2 – Punishment

refs.q: Specifically, how much was lawfully acquired, the offender’s interest in it, and the extent it was used to facilitate the offence are all relevant and may require proof.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation > 17.2 – Interaction with sentencing principles and purposes > 17.2.2 – Punishment

title: Confiscation appeals; fresh evidence of true impact
statement: Anyone with an interest may appeal a forfeiture order or PPO (or refusal) as if part of the sentence; it may be confirmed, discharged, varied or remitted. Where the true impact emerges after sentence, it may be fresh evidence enlivening resentencing.

refs.q: A person with an interest in property in respect of which a forfeiture order or pecuniary penalty order has been made or refused may appeal against the order or refusal in the same manner as if the order were part of the sentence imposed.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation > 17.3 – Appeals

refs.q: Where the true impact of a confiscation order becomes apparent after sentence, this may constitute fresh evidence and enliven an appellate court’s discretion to resentence the offender.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation > 17.3 – Appeals

refs.q: On appeal, the order or refusal may be confirmed, discharged or varied or the matter may be remitted for rehearing.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 17 – Confiscation > 17.3 – Appeals

title: Compensation orders: civil, ancillary, additional to sentence
statement: Courts may order compensation for personal injury and property loss or damage, and restitution of property. Compensation is additional to sentence — a convenient mechanism for victims; an application is a civil proceeding ancillary to sentencing on the civil standard. The VOCA Act scheme operates independently and is not considered in the Manual. The Act has two independent, parallel schemes (personal injury; property).

refs.q: Compensation is ordered in addition to imposing sentence and is intended to provide a convenient mechanism for a victim to recover compensation. An application seeking compensation is a civil proceeding, ancillary to sentencing, to which the civil standard of proof applies.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders

refs.q: That scheme operates independently of the sentencing hearing and is not considered in this manual.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders

refs.q: The Sentencing Act 1991 (Vic) (‘the Act’) establishes two independent and parallel compensation schemes for victims of crime who have suffered personal injury and property damage.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.1 – Compensation orders > 18.1.1 – Threshold requirements

refs.q: A court may make compensatory orders for personal injury, property loss or damage, and restitution of property.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders

refs.q: The Victims of Crime Assistance Act 1996 (Vic) (‘VOCA Act’) also enacts a complementary scheme, which provides for compensation to victims out of consolidated revenue up to certain statutory limits.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders

refs.q: There are some requirements specific to each.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.1 – Compensation orders > 18.1.1 – Threshold requirements

title: Personal injury compensation: who, what injury, time limits
statement: A guilty or convicted person may be ordered to compensate someone who suffered any injury as a direct result of the offending (including other occurrences within a representative charge). “Injury” is defined as physical harm; mental illness or disorder (or exacerbation); pregnancy; grief, distress, trauma or other significant adverse effect; combinations — but not property loss. Only on application by the injured person (or on their behalf: for children or incapable persons; the DPP, informant or police prosecutor in the Magistrates’ Court; the DPP otherwise). Apply within 12 months after the finding of guilt or conviction (extendable in the interests of justice — viewed liberally, the court balancing finality and rehabilitation against the rights of victims; for a guilty plea time appears to run from sentence; for a person who has been convicted the Manual says it is unclear whether time runs from plea or finding of guilt or from sentence, although a person is generally “convicted” when the verdict or plea is accepted: flag.compensation_time_limit_start). Extension considerations: likely success in time; length of and reasons for delay; prejudice to rehabilitation; forensic disadvantage.

refs.q: A guilty or “convicted” person may be ordered to pay compensation to someone who has suffered any injury as a direct result of their offending, which includes any other occurrence of the same offence involved in the course of conduct of a representative or sample charge.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.1 – Compensation orders > 18.1.1 – Threshold requirements > 18.1.1.1 – Personal injury compensation

refs.q: ‘Injury’ is defined as: • actual physical bodily harm; or • mental illness or disorder, or its exacerbation, whether or not flowing from nervous shock; or • pregnancy; or • grief, distress or trauma or other significant adverse effect; or • any combination arising from an offence but not including injury due to loss of or damage to property.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.1 – Compensation orders > 18.1.1 – Threshold requirements > 18.1.1.1 – Personal injury compensation

refs.q: A compensation order for personal injury may only be made on application by the injured person
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.1 – Compensation orders > 18.1.1 – Threshold requirements > 18.1.1.1 – Personal injury compensation

refs.q: An application for personal injury must be made within 12 months after the offender is found guilty or convicted of the offence, and may be extended on application or by the court’s own motion if the court believes it is in the interests of justice to do so.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.1 – Compensation orders > 18.1.1 – Threshold requirements > 18.1.1.1 – Personal injury compensation

refs.q: However, for someone who pleads guilty, it appears that for the purposes of the Act, the time runs from the date they are sentenced.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.1 – Compensation orders > 18.1.1 – Threshold requirements > 18.1.1.1 – Personal injury compensation

refs.q: • whether the order would have succeeded if brought within time; • the length of delay in comparison to other cases; • the reasons for delay, and whether the applicant took prompt action to apply; • whether the delay would significantly prejudice the offender’s rehabilitation; • whether the delay will cause forensic disadvantage to the offender.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.1 – Compensation orders > 18.1.1 – Threshold requirements > 18.1.1.1 – Personal injury compensation

refs.q: For someone who has been convicted it is unclear if the limitation period begins to run after a plea or finding of guilt, or upon the imposition of sentence.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.1 – Compensation orders > 18.1.1 – Threshold requirements > 18.1.1.1 – Personal injury compensation

refs.q: Generally, a person is “convicted” when the trial judge accepts the jury’s verdict or by some action accepts the offender’s plea of guilty.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.1 – Compensation orders > 18.1.1 – Threshold requirements > 18.1.1.1 – Personal injury compensation

refs.q: An application may be made by the injured person, or on their behalf: • by any person other than the offender if the victim is a child, or is incapable of making the application due to injury, disease, senility, illness or physical or mental impairment; • by the Director of Public Prosecutions (‘DPP’), the informant or police prosecutor if the sentencing court was the Magistrates' Court; or • by the DPP if the sentencing court was not the Magistrates' Court.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.1 – Compensation orders > 18.1.1 – Threshold requirements > 18.1.1.1 – Personal injury compensation

refs.q: The court will consider the circumstances of the application, such as: • whether the order would have succeeded if brought within time; • the length of delay in comparison to other cases; • the reasons for delay, and whether the applicant took prompt action to apply; • whether the delay would significantly prejudice the offender’s rehabilitation; • whether the delay will cause forensic disadvantage to the offender.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.1 – Compensation orders > 18.1.1 – Threshold requirements > 18.1.1.1 – Personal injury compensation

refs.q: Examples where time has been extended include where injuries are insidious, such as with some psychological disorders, but ultimately each decision turns on its own facts.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.1 – Compensation orders > 18.1.1 – Threshold requirements > 18.1.1.1 – Personal injury compensation

title: Property loss or damage compensation: application, court’s inquiry, own motion, timing
statement: On the victim’s application (or by the DPP; or DPP, informant or police prosecutor in the Magistrates’ Court). Where evidence of property loss or damage is presented the court must ask the prosecution whether an application will be made (its failure to ask does not prevent an application). The court may act on its own motion if the beneficiary does not oppose and the offender has been heard — but only for offences whose hearing commenced on or after 31 January 2013. Apply as soon as practicable (interpreted broadly, but no open-ended right; waiting to assess means is not as soon as practicable).

refs.q: If a court finds a person guilty or convicts them of an offence, and evidence is presented that loss, destruction or damage to property has occurred as a result, the court must ask the prosecution if an application for a compensation order will be made.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.1 – Compensation orders > 18.1.1 – Threshold requirements > 18.1.1.2 – Property loss or damage

refs.q: • the person in whose favour the order is to be made does not oppose it; and • the court has given the offender the opportunity to be heard in respect of the order.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.1 – Compensation orders > 18.1.1 – Threshold requirements > 18.1.1.2 – Property loss or damage

refs.q: The application must be made as soon as practicable after the offender is found guilty or convicted of the offence.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.1 – Compensation orders > 18.1.1 – Threshold requirements > 18.1.1.2 – Property loss or damage

refs.q: For example, waiting to determine if the offender has the financial means to pay before making the application would not be considered ‘as soon as practicable’.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.1 – Compensation orders > 18.1.1 – Threshold requirements > 18.1.1.2 – Property loss or damage

refs.q: The court may only make an order on its own motion in respect of offences for which the hearing of the charge commences on or after 31 January 2013:
Failure by the court to ask the prosecution does not prevent a person applying for a compensation order:

An order may also be made on the court’s own motion where: • the person in whose favour the order is to be made does not oppose it; and • the court has given the offender the opportunity to be heard in respect of the order.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.1 – Compensation orders > 18.1.1 – Threshold requirements > 18.1.1.2 – Property loss or damage

refs.q: An order may be made on the application of the victim, by the DPP on their behalf (in higher courts), or by the DPP, informant or police prosecutor on their behalf (in the Magistrates’ Court).
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.1 – Compensation orders > 18.1.1 – Threshold requirements > 18.1.1.2 – Property loss or damage

title: Compensation: procedural fairness; facts must sufficiently appear; clear cases only
statement: Procedural fairness applies; evidence may be given and tested. The court must hear and determine the application unless the relevant facts (commission, identity, injuries, impact, special expenses, causation) do not sufficiently appear; undisputed prosecution statements of facts and documentary evidence may be used. Orders suit only clear cases; significant unresolved factual conflicts, contribution and joint/several liability questions may make it too complex (leaving civil remedies), though the victim’s burden of civil proceedings is weighed.

refs.q: It is important to note at the outset that all requirements of procedural fairness apply to compensation proceedings.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.1 – Compensation orders > 18.1.2 – Process

refs.q: Firstly, a court must hear and determine a compensation application unless the relevant facts do not sufficiently appear from specific documents, statements, or evidence.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.1 – Compensation orders > 18.1.3 – Considerations

refs.q: As compensation orders are intended to provide a simple process for the benefit of claimants, the discretion to make a compensation order should be exercised only in clear cases.

refs.q: Conversely, where there are still significant and unresolved conflicts over the facts after the trial, the parties should be left to their civil remedies.

title: Compensation: assessing the amount (synthesis; means; rehabilitation; no punitive damages; children $1000)
statement: The court intuitively synthesises seriousness, relationships, degree of injury, the offender’s financial circumstances, the effect on rehabilitation and the burden of payment. Means are relevant, not controlling; inability to discover means does not prevent an order. Balance compensation against rehabilitation (and denunciation). Child offenders cannot be ordered above $1000 and their means must be considered. Amounts follow common law damages principles (possibly contributory negligence) with heads expanded by statute; no punitive damages; amounts may be reduced to avoid over-compensation where claims cannot be tested (no blanket discount). Joint offenders: apportionment (not automatic) or joint and several liability; complexity may justify declining.

refs.q: • seriousness of the offending; • relationship between the offence and the victim, and the victim and the offender; • degree of injury suffered by the victim; • offender’s financial circumstances; • effect of a compensation order on the offender’s prospects for rehabilitation; and • nature of the burden that payment will impose.

title: Compensation: heads of claim, causation, grief factors, property value cap, discounts, method and costs
statement: Personal injury heads: pain and suffering; reasonable counselling, medical and other non-property expenses (incurred or likely). “Direct result” uses tort causation and remoteness (a significant role or substantial operating cause; may develop gradually or appear later; feelings about the trial are too tenuous). Grief factors: circumstances of death, effect on hearing, closeness, applicant’s age, extent of suffering. Property compensation cannot exceed the property’s value; no order if property is recovered without loss. Reduce by VOCA awards (same head) and amounts repaid; avoid double compensation. Instalments may be ordered. Each party bears its own costs unless the court orders otherwise.

refs.q: The requirement that the injury be the ‘direct result of the offence’ does not mean that the offence must be the sole cause of the injury. It should be assessed according to common law tort principles of causation and remoteness and not extend further.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.1 – Compensation orders > 18.1.4 – Assessing amount and method of payment > 18.1.4.2 – Assessing personal injury claim

refs.q: • the circumstances in which the death occurred; • the effect on the applicant on hearing of the events causing loss; • the closeness of the relationship between the person seeking compensation and the person who has been killed; • the age of the person seeking compensation; and • the extent of grief and psychological suffering experienced as a result of the loss.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.1 – Compensation orders > 18.1.4 – Assessing amount and method of payment > 18.1.4.2 – Assessing personal injury claim

refs.q: Because the power to compensate is enlivened only if the victim suffers loss, where property is recovered and returned without any loss to the owner, there is no basis for a compensation order.

refs.q: The extent of compensation will be determined as the court thinks fit but must not exceed the value of the property lost, destroyed or damaged.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.1 – Compensation orders > 18.1.4 – Assessing amount and method of payment > 18.1.4.3 – Assessing property loss or damage claim

refs.q: For personal injury compensation orders, any amount ordered must be reduced by any compensation awarded under the VOCA Act. This is designed to prevent double compensation of victims of crime.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.1 – Compensation orders > 18.1.4 – Assessing amount and method of payment > 18.1.4.4 – Discounting and limiting factors

refs.q: It is also usual for the quantum of compensation to be reduced by amounts already repaid.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.1 – Compensation orders > 18.1.4 – Assessing amount and method of payment > 18.1.4.4 – Discounting and limiting factors

refs.q: The court may direct that payment be made by instalments, and any default will cause the outstanding amount to become due and payable.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.1 – Compensation orders > 18.1.4 – Assessing amount and method of payment > 18.1.4.5 – Method

refs.q: All parties bear their own costs of a compensation proceeding unless the court orders otherwise.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.1 – Compensation orders > 18.1.5 – Costs

refs.q: A compensation order may consist of amounts for: • pain and suffering experienced by the victim; • some or all expenses incurred, or reasonably likely to be incurred, by the victim for: • reasonable counselling services; • medical expenses; or • any other expenses not relating to property loss or damage.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.1 – Compensation orders > 18.1.4 – Assessing amount and method of payment > 18.1.4.2 – Assessing personal injury claim

refs.q: An injury may be directly caused by a crime notwithstanding that it: • develops gradually; • becomes manifest only after a lapse of time; or • is revealed only by expert diagnosis of multiple symptoms (especially with psychological or mental injury.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.1 – Compensation orders > 18.1.4 – Assessing amount and method of payment > 18.1.4.2 – Assessing personal injury claim

refs.q: However, while feelings about the trial process may arguably be ‘compensable injury’, they would not be caused ‘as a direct result of the offence’ but are instead tenuously related.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.1 – Compensation orders > 18.1.4 – Assessing amount and method of payment > 18.1.4.2 – Assessing personal injury claim

title: Compensation: combination with sanctions; priority over fines; appeal; judgment debt
statement: A compensation order is an independent discretionary consequence; it may accompany dismissals, discharges and adjournments and offences taken into account; it cannot be a condition of a CCO (but may accompany one as an ancillary order). The Manual says compensation orders are “relevant to assessing whether to impose a fine” (the court must consider their effect on the offender’s finances), while 12.3.1 says finances are irrelevant to whether to fine and are considered only after deciding to fine (flag.compensation_whether_to_fine; (app policy) compensation is treated as reducing the means available for a fine’s amount and payment, not as deciding whether to fine). If the offender cannot pay both, compensation has priority. It is “considered a sentence” under the Criminal Procedure Act, so an appeal is an appeal against sentence (leave required). Compensation and restitution orders are not regarded as punitive and so are not considered as punishment in sentencing (7.7.1, contrasting confiscation orders), though their effect on the offender’s finances bears on a fine (above); (app policy) it is not counted in the maxima or s 6AAA checks. It is a judgment debt; civil rights are unaffected.

refs.q: Compensation orders may be made in addition to dismissals, discharges and adjournments, and can also be made in respect of offences taken into account.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.1 – Compensation orders > 18.1.6 – Impacts

refs.q: Compensation orders cannot be made as a condition of a CCO, but can be made in the usual fashion as an ancillary order to sentence.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.1 – Compensation orders > 18.1.6 – Impacts

refs.q: Where the court intends to impose a fine and a compensation order, but the offender has insufficient means to pay both, the compensation order must be given priority.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.1 – Compensation orders > 18.1.6 – Impacts

refs.q: An appeal against such an order is, consequently, an appeal against sentence, for which leave is required.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.1 – Compensation orders > 18.1.6 – Impacts

refs.q: A compensation order, including any costs ordered, must be taken to be a judgment debt due by the offender to the person in whose favour the order is made.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.1 – Compensation orders > 18.1.6 – Impacts

refs.q: Compensation orders are relevant to assessing whether to impose a fine, in that the court must consider the effect of any compensation order on the financial circumstances of the offender.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.1 – Compensation orders > 18.1.6 – Impacts

refs.q: A compensation order is considered a sentence under the Criminal Procedure Act 2009 (Vic).
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.1 – Compensation orders > 18.1.6 – Impacts

refs.q: By contrast compensation and restitution orders, which benefit private victims of crime, are not regarded as punitive and are not considered.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.7 – Punishment from ancillary orders > 7.7.1 – Forfeiture and pecuniary penalty orders

title: Restitution orders (stolen goods)
statement: Where goods are stolen and a person is found guilty of a connected offence, the court may order return of the goods or replacement goods, payment of their value from money in the offender’s possession at arrest, or payment to good-faith purchasers or lenders. Orders are for relatively straightforward cases (otherwise civil remedies) and require facts established by evidence, available documents or admissions. They may be combined with community-based orders, dismissals, discharges and adjournments, and offences taken into account; they are “relevant to assessing whether to impose a fine” through their effect on the offender’s finances (see flag.compensation_whether_to_fine); prefer restitution over a fine if both cannot be paid. A money order is enforceable as a judgment debt and its payment takes priority over other civil orders and fines. Victims cannot appeal a restitution decision.

refs.q: Under the Act a court has discretion to make a Restitution Order (‘RES Order’) where goods have been stolen, and a person has been found guilty or convicted of an offence connected with the theft.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.2 – Restitution

refs.q: A RES Order is intended for straightforward cases, and the discretion should not be exercised where civil remedies may be better suited to do justice between parties.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.2 – Restitution > 18.2.1 – Process

refs.q: A RES Order may be combined with other sanctions, such as a community-based order, dismissals, discharges and adjournments. RES Orders can also be made in respect of offences taken into account.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.2 – Restitution > 18.2.2 – Combination with other sanctions

refs.q: If the court considers that the offender cannot pay both a fine and a RES Order, and it is appropriate to impose both, a court must give preference to a RES Order.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 18 – Compensatory orders > 18.2 – Restitution > 18.2.2 – Combination with other sanctions

title: Forensic sample orders: not part of the sentence; forensic sample offences
statement: A forensic sample order directs a procedure to take a sample; commonly made at sentence but not part of it. Available on a finding of guilt for a forensic sample offence (or conspiracy, incitement or attempt), for any relevant finding of guilt after 1 July 1998 (and also for findings before 1 July 1998 where the offender was detained, then or later, for any other offence). A “forensic sample offence” is any indictable offence or a Schedule 8 offence for findings after 1 July 2014; for findings before 1 July 2014 the definition then in force applies (the Manual’s wording leaves a finding on 1 July 2014 itself uncovered: flag.forensic_definition_date). The prosecution applies; the order is discretionary. Samples already taken from adults are automatically retained (subject to requirements). State provisions do not apply to Commonwealth offences.

refs.q: A forensic sample order directs a person to undergo a procedure to take a forensic sample from any part of their body. These orders are commonly made at the time of sentencing but do not form part of the sentence.

refs.q: An order may be made following a finding of guilt for a forensic sample offence (or of conspiracy or incitement to commit or attempting to commit a forensic sample offence).

title: Forensic sample orders: application, time limits, hearing, determination, reasons, review, retention
statement: Application usually by police (DPP in higher courts) specifying intimate or non-intimate sample; notice required for child offenders. Time: any time after the finding of guilt but no later than six months after the appeal period (or appeal determination); a 12-month limit applies in narrow circumstances to certain old drug offences. The offender is not a party and cannot call or cross-examine witnesses (adults may only respond to the court’s inquiries; children may address seriousness and justification). The court must consider the seriousness of the circumstances of the offence and be satisfied the order is justified in all the circumstances (the seriousness of the circumstances is the only mandated consideration; beyond it the discretion is very broad: recidivism risk is a common circumstance, the gravity of the offending may justify an order even without that risk, and social utility may also be relevant). The court must give reasons, serve the order and reasons, and inform that reasonable force may be used. Not appealable as part of sentence (judicial review). No order is needed to retain a sample already taken from an adult who is found guilty (or not guilty because of mental impairment) of one of the listed indictable offences; it may then be retained indefinitely, and must be destroyed if that finding is set aside on appeal unless retained for non-identifying statistical purposes. A retention order for a child requires a finding of guilt of the offence for which the procedure was conducted, an offence arising out of the same circumstances, or an offence on which evidence from the procedure had probative value, and an application within six months of the appeal period; retention orders for children follow the same considerations, and the same process applies on a finding of not guilty because of mental impairment, but not to an offence heard and determined summarily (19.4.2; whether that exclusion covers only the mental-impairment extension is not clear).

refs.q: An application must specify the type of sample (whether intimate or non-intimate) sought to be taken in the forensic procedure.

title: Alcohol exclusion orders (Sentencing Act): mandatory when criteria met
statement: A court must make an AEO if it records a conviction for a relevant offence and is satisfied on the balance of probabilities that the offender was intoxicated — defined as speech, balance, coordination or behaviour noticeably affected by the consumption of liquor (not drugs) — and that the intoxication significantly contributed, and the offender is not and has not been subject to a previous AEO for the current offence. AEOs last two years (from release if combined with or during custody; otherwise from the making of the order). Relevant offences are described by category (homicide, causing injury, administering substances, threats, endangering, kidnap and assault, certain resisting arrest and assisting offender offences, firearm use, certain adult and child sexual offences, CAM offences) and are not mapped to register ids, so (app policy) membership must be confirmed where the offence is not plainly within a category. An AEO prohibits consuming or attempting to consume liquor in licensed premises and entering or remaining at major events; exemptions are permitted for good reason where otherwise appropriate. With an AEO the court may not also make an EO or attach an alcohol exclusion condition to a CCO, but may combine an AEO with a CCO. Contravention: maximum Level 7 imprisonment. An AEO is capable of being punitive because it restrains liberty in addition to a sentence of imprisonment; those restraints are part of the circumstances the court must generally consider in the synthesis, and any further punitive element depends on the offender’s circumstances. Its punitive effect on sentence follows the principles printed at 11.4.2.8 (“The following principles apply to an alcohol exclusion order”; flag.aeo_principles_placement): an offender contending for additional punitive impact must say so expressly, with evidence, addressing the s 89DE(5) exemption, and the court should then make a finding and explain its effect.
logic: AEO required (error if missing) only if: conviction recorded ∧ relevant offence ∧ intoxicated by liquor (balance of probabilities) ∧ intoxication significantly contributed ∧ no previous AEO for the offence; any element unknown (including whether the offence is a relevant offence, or whether the intoxication was by liquor) → caution, not error

title: Compensation: extensions of time; “as soon as practicable”; order of the inquiry; facts that must be easily determined
statement: On an extension of time for personal injury compensation the court balances finality and rehabilitation against victims’ rights, viewing out-of-time applications liberally (a criminal, not civil, statute) but not permitting late applications that may significantly prejudice rehabilitation. For property, “as soon as practicable” depends on the circumstances and is read broadly for the claimant, but there is no open-ended right. Once compensation is applied for, the court first considers whether to grant it before the amount, and also whether the case is too complex; it should be able to determine the listed matters easily (including each offender’s order reflecting their individual contribution to the victim’s pain and suffering, and the offenders’ financial circumstances and burden — though an order may be made despite an inability to discover them). Difficulty may mean the facts do not sufficiently appear or the issues are too complex; no information may indicate the facts do not appear.

title: Compensation amount: the synthesis; the offender’s circumstances and rehabilitation; untested claims; pain and suffering; causation; grief
statement: Where there is an entitlement the court intuitively synthesises all the material circumstances (the listed matters). It may look at the offender’s personal circumstances (character, antecedents, age, health and any custodial burden) in assessing the burden, and most importantly the burden on rehabilitation. Because offenders may not be able to fully test the claims, the amount should give the victim “an appropriate measure of justice without running the risk of doing injustice to the offender”. “Pain and suffering” is undefined and assessed by intuition and experience. Causation: the damage must be reasonably foreseeable and not tenuously related; “direct” does not mean immediate, proximate or obvious — the crime must play a significant role or be a substantial and operating cause — assessed in a common-sense way (injury may be directly caused despite extraneous contributions, such as earlier abuse). Grief or trauma is assessed by the listed factors; the award is highly discretionary and views will differ widely. Depending on the circumstances the court may order no or reduced compensation, defer payment or order instalments; alternatively, it may order full compensation regardless of the offender’s circumstances, as long as they are taken into account.

refs.q: Where a court concludes there is an entitlement to compensation, whether for personal injury or property loss, it must intuitively synthesise all the material circumstances of the case, including the: • seriousness of the offending; • relationship between the offence and the victim, and the victim and the offender; • degree of injury suffered by the victim; • offender’s financial circumstances; • effect of a compensation order on the offender’s prospects for rehabilitation; and • nature of the burden that payment will impose.

title: Compensation: fire-fighting costs excluded; overlapping awards; Wrongs Act provisions; instalments; costs
statement: Compensable “property” may include motor vehicles and inheritances, but not a public authority’s costs of extinguishing a fire. Where awards overlap for the same head of damage the amount is reduced (the rest untouched); for overlaps not prescribed by legislation the court may reduce to avoid double payment, especially where the offender is serving a life sentence. After describing Part VBA of the Wrongs Act (thresholds for non-economic loss) the Manual says “These provisions do not apply to orders under the Act” (whether this covers only Part VBA or the Wrongs Act provisions generally is not stated: flag.wrongs_act_provisions_referent). A debtor may apply for an instalment order under the Judgment Debt Recovery Act 1984 s 6 even if the court did not order instalments. On costs the court considers the impact on the victim, complexity, the number of offences against the applicant, the time between offending and the award, the need for proper representation and the need for specialist medical opinions.

title: Restitution: the available orders; combined orders; timing; appeals and stays; when to leave parties to civil remedies
statement: A restitution order may direct that the goods be returned to the entitled person; that replacement goods (goods that “directly or indirectly represent the stolen goods”) be returned; that the goods’ value be paid to the entitled person from money in the offender’s possession at arrest; or that the purchase price be paid from that money to a third party who bought the goods in good faith or lent money on their security. Where goods are intermingled, only the parts that were stolen may be ordered restored. A combined order for replacement goods and money is allowed if the entitled person does not recover more than the goods’ value. Apply as soon as practicable after the finding of guilt or conviction. The offender may appeal, or the DPP where there is an error and it is in the public interest; a Supreme or County Court order is stayed during the appeal period unless otherwise directed. Parties should be left to civil remedies where there are significant factual conflicts requiring a complicated or extensive inquiry, where the evidentiary limits in s 84(8) cause difficulty, or where taking accounts or moulding equitable relief is required.

refs.q: A court may order that: • the goods be returned to the person entitled to them (‘entitled person’); • goods which ‘directly or indirectly represent the stolen goods’ (‘replacement goods’) be returned to the entitled person; • the value of the stolen goods be paid to the entitled person out of money in the offender’s possession at the time of arrest; • the purchase price of the stolen goods be paid to a third party out of money in the offender’s possession at the time of arrest, if the stolen goods were purchased in good faith or money lent on the security of the stolen goods.

title: Alcohol exclusion orders: comparison-table criteria; application timing; content; exemptions and variation; the prohibitions
statement: In the Manual’s comparison table, the AEO column requires a recorded conviction for a relevant offence, no previous AEO for the offence circumstances, and satisfaction on the balance of probabilities that the offender was intoxicated and the intoxication significantly contributed; its conditions include a prohibition on consuming alcohol. The application must be filed and served before the first mention, committal mention or first directions hearing (or later with leave). An AEO must contain the offender’s name, the grounds, the prohibited conduct and any exemptions, and when it takes effect and its duration; exemptions (e.g. for weddings or sporting events) should be detailed. The court may vary an AEO if satisfied that new facts or circumstances have arisen and that there is a good reason why the offender should or should not be allowed to enter specified premises or an event, and it considers the variation appropriate; it may impose, vary or remove exemptions and must specify when the varied AEO takes effect. An AEO offender must not knowingly or recklessly enter, remain or attempt to in a prohibited place, or consume or attempt to consume liquor in licensed premises; it is not a contravention if caused by circumstances beyond their control and they took reasonable precautions.

title: LCRA exclusion orders: specified offences; the effectiveness considerations; the prohibitions
statement: Specified offences include causing injury and assault; threats, endangering conduct and administering substances; being armed with criminal intent and prohibited weapons; rape and sexual assault; destroying or damaging property; and offensive and obscene behaviour, disorderly conduct and failing to leave licensed premises. To decide whether an EO may be an effective and reasonable deterrent the court must consider the nature and gravity of the specified offence; prior findings of guilt for a specified offence in the designated area; any EO for another specified offence; the likely impact on the offender, any victim, public safety and public order; and any other relevant matter. An EO offender must not enter, re-enter or attempt to enter the designated area or licensed premises, and on contravening must obey a police officer’s lawful direction to leave. The offender, the DPP or a police officer may apply to the court that made the EO to vary it; the court may vary it in any way it considers appropriate if satisfied that facts or circumstances have arisen since the order (or its last variation) that make variation appropriate.

refs.q: A ‘specified offence’ includes: • causing injury and assault offences; • threat offences, endangering conduct and administering substances offences; • being armed with criminal intent and prohibited weapons offences; • rape and sexual assault offences; • destroying or damaging property offences; and • offensive and obscene behaviour offences, disorderly conduct and failure to leave licensed premises.

refs.q: To determine if an EO might be an effective and reasonable deterrent, a court must consider: • the nature and gravity of the specified offence; • whether the offender has previously been found guilty of a specified offence committed in the designated area; • whether the offender is or has been the subject of an EO in relation to another specified offence committed in the same or another designated area; • the likely impact of the EO on the offender, any victim, public safety, and public order; and • any other matter it considers relevant.

title: Victorian identity crime certificates: the “ID offence”; the certificate’s contents
statement: An ID offence uses identification information that does not relate to the offender. The certificate must identify the ID offence, the victim’s name and anything else the court considers relevant.

refs.q: An ID offence uses identification information (‘ID info’) that does not relate to the offender.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 20 – Other ancillary orders > 20.2 – Identity crime certificates > 20.2.1 – Victorian certificates

refs.q: The certificate must identify the ID offence, the victim’s name, and anything else the court considers relevant.
refs.path: Part D – Ancillary Proceedings and Orders > 20 – Other ancillary orders > 20.2 – Identity crime certificates > 20.2.1 – Victorian certificates

refs.q: ID info means information relating to a person (whether living, dead, real, or fictitious) that is capable of being used (alone or in conjunction with other information) to identify or purportedly identify the person. This includes: • a name, address, date of birth or place of birth; • information on a person’s marital status or that identifies another person as a relative of the person; • a driver licence or driver licence number, passport or passport number; • biometric data, a voice print or a digital signature; • a credit or debit card, its number, or data stored or encrypted on it; • a financial account number, username or password; • a series of numbers or letters (or both) intended for use as a means of personal identification; or • an Australian Business Number.
